newsitem.title: ITALY: MOTOR RACING-CONTROVERSIAL SENNA DEATH TRIAL SET TO START.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-CONTROVERSIAL SENNA DEATH TRIAL SET TO START.

text.p: Formula One team chief Frank Williams and five other people go on trial on Thursday charged with manslaughter over the death of Brazilian Ayrton Senna, one of the greatest drivers in motor racing history.
The case has sent shock waves through the glamorous Formula One circuit and top racing crews have warned they will not risk competing in Italian events if the six men are found guilty.
Triple world champion Senna suffered fatal head injuries when his Williams car hurtled into a concrete wall at around 220 kph during the San Marino Grand Prix on May 1, 1994.

Italian state prosecutors believe the steering column on 32-year-old Senna's car snapped as a result of a poor weld when the vehicle tried to turn Imola's infamous Tamburello curve while leading the field into the seventh lap.

The defendants, who include Williams' technical director Patrick Head and designer Adrian Newey, deny any responsibility. They will not attend Thursday's opening session, which will focus on legal technicalities.
First witnesses are due to be heard next month and a spokeswoman for the Williams team said Frank Williams would probably not appear at the trial until the end of April.

The high-profile case, which is being heard in a makeshift courtroom in this picturesque northern Italian town, is scheduled to last three months but one legal source close to Williams said he did not foresee a verdict until the autumn.
Manslaughter carries a maximum jail sentence of five years in Italy, but the legal source said that in the event of a conviction he would expect at most a suspended term.
That would be small comfort for the British-based Williams team, which hopes to establish that Senna's steering column snapped after the high speed smash and not before.

"I think, for any design engineer, this is very serious," Head told reporters last week. "It's not something I want on my record, and I am prepared, if the case goes against us, to appeal and fight for as long as necessary to clear my name."

The Sunday Times newspaper published a photograph at the weekend showing a small piece of debris in Senna's path moments before he crashed, and said the Brazilian ace might have lost control of his car while trying to avoid the fragment.

The public prosecutor who has led the investigations, Maurizio Passarini, denied the suggestion. He will use high-tech computer graphics in court to try to persuade judge Antonio Costanzo that faulty Williams engineering caused the smash.
Racing authorities have expressed dismay at the trial and warned that teams might not come to Italy if management faced conviction in the event of accidents.
"Fatality is part of the game," Flavio Briatore, head of the Benetton Formula One team, said last December.

Belgian international race director Roland Bruynseraede, Imola track manager Federico Bendinelli and track director Giorgio Poggi are also accused of manslaughter for allowing the race to go ahead on an allegedly unsafe circuit.

The ill-fated 1994 Grand Prix was marred by tragedy. Besides Senna, Austrian driver Roland Ratzenberger also died after a 300-kph crash during testing. Their deaths were the first fatalities at a grand prix for 12 years.

However, the International Automobile Federation (FIA) has stood by its race staff. "This is a uniquely Italian problem requiring a uniquely Italian solution," FIA president Max Mosley said last year.
Four cases over the last 40 years involving fatal crashes at Italian motor events all ended in acquitals.
